questions.stem: The gas chiefly responsible for the depletion of the ozone layer is:

options.option_text: Carbon dioxide
Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)
Methane
Sulphur dioxide

questions.explanation: CFCs — used in old refrigerators, aerosols and foam-blowing agents — release chlorine radicals in the stratosphere that destroy ozone. The 1985 Vienna Convention and the 1987 Montreal Protocol phased them out; the ozone hole over Antarctica has since been gradually recovering. CO₂, CH₄, N₂O are greenhouse gases that drive climate change, not ozone depletion. SO₂ drives acid rain.

questions.stem: The Air Quality Index (AQI) in India uses a six-category colour scale from 'Good' to 'Severe'. The highest 'Severe' category begins at an AQI value of:
questions.explanation: CPCB's National AQI (2014) scale — Good 0-50, Satisfactory 51-100, Moderate 101-200, Poor 201-300, Very Poor 301-400, Severe 401-500. AQI above 500 is sometimes reported as 'Severe+ / Emergency'. 8 pollutants tracked — PM2.5, PM10, NO₂, SO₂, CO, O₃, NH₃, Pb. Delhi regularly tops the world's worst-air cities list in winter.

questions.stem: Fine particulate matter that poses the greatest health risk — PM2.5 — is defined as airborne particles of diameter less than:

options.option_text: 25 µm
2.5 µm
25 nm

questions.explanation: PM2.5 — particulate matter ≤ 2.5 micrometres (µm) in aerodynamic diameter. Small enough to reach the alveoli and the bloodstream. Main sources: vehicle exhaust, coal-fired plants, stubble burning, wood / dung fires. WHO's 2021 annual PM2.5 guideline is 5 µg/m³; India's national standard is 40 µg/m³. PM10 is larger coarse-fraction particulate. 25 µm is the rough size of a fine grain of sand.

questions.stem: The most abundant greenhouse gas by mass in Earth's atmosphere — though it is also part of the natural water cycle — is:

options.option_text: Carbon dioxide
Water vapour
Methane
Nitrous oxide

questions.explanation: Water vapour is the single largest greenhouse gas by mass and accounts for the bulk of the natural greenhouse effect (+33 °C compared to a no-atmosphere baseline). However, in climate-change discussions the focus is on CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O because these are the gases humans are adding; water vapour adjusts to temperature (a positive feedback, but not a forcing). Methane (from paddy, livestock, leaks) is ~25× stronger per molecule than CO₂.

questions.stem: The Bhopal gas tragedy of December 1984 was caused by leakage of which toxic gas?

options.option_text: Chlorine
Methyl isocyanate
Ammonia
Sulphur dioxide

questions.explanation: On the night of 2/3 December 1984, about 40 tonnes of methyl isocyanate (MIC) leaked from a Union Carbide India Ltd pesticide plant in Bhopal, killing at least 3,800 people immediately and over 15,000 in the aftermath. It remains the world's worst industrial disaster. The case led to the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 and the 1991 Public Liability Insurance Act.

questions.stem: Photochemical smog in cities is primarily formed by the action of sunlight on:

options.option_text: CO₂ and H₂O vapour
NOₓ and volatile organic compounds (VOCs)
CH₄ and CO
SO₂ and H₂S

questions.explanation: Photochemical smog — first seen in Los Angeles in the 1940s — forms when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds from vehicle exhaust react with ultraviolet light to produce ground-level ozone and peroxyacetyl nitrates (PAN). These irritate eyes and lungs. Classic 'London smog' (1952) was SO₂ + particulate smoke + fog — the deadly killer 'pea-souper' that led to the UK's Clean Air Act 1956.

questions.stem: The ozone layer lies in which layer of the Earth's atmosphere?

options.option_text: Troposphere
Stratosphere
Mesosphere
Thermosphere

questions.explanation: The ozone layer sits in the stratosphere (~15-35 km above the surface). There, ozone absorbs most of the Sun's harmful UV-B radiation, shielding life. Troposphere — the lowest layer, where weather happens (up to ~12 km). Mesosphere (50-85 km) — where meteors burn up. Thermosphere (85-600 km) — where auroras occur and the ISS orbits.

questions.stem: In urban areas, the primary anthropogenic source of carbon monoxide (CO) in the ambient atmosphere is:

options.option_text: Volcanic emissions releasing sulphur and carbon gases
Incomplete combustion of fossil fuels in vehicles
Decomposition of organic matter in wetlands and soil
Evaporation of industrial solvents and paint thinners

questions.explanation: B is correct because CO is produced when carbon-based fuels burn without sufficient oxygen — the classic condition in internal combustion engines and two-wheelers. CO binds to haemoglobin ~200× more readily than O₂, making vehicle exhaust its chief urban health hazard. Option A (volcanic emissions) is a natural, not anthropogenic, source and contributes mainly SO₂. Option C is the pathway for methane (CH₄), not CO.

questions.stem: Precipitation is classified as 'acid rain' because normal rainwater is already mildly acidic. The pH threshold below which rain is formally considered acidic is:

options.option_text: pH 7.0 — the neutral point of pure distilled water
pH 6.5 — the WHO standard for drinking water safety
pH 5.6 — normal rainwater acidity from dissolved CO₂
pH 4.5 — the threshold for visible forest damage onset

questions.explanation: C is correct because atmospheric CO₂ dissolves in rainwater forming carbonic acid, giving clean rain a natural pH of ~5.6. Any lower pH (caused by SO₂ or NOₓ forming sulphuric/nitric acid) qualifies as acid rain. Option A (7.0) is wrong — neutral pH is not the correct baseline since unpolluted rain is already slightly acidic. Option D (4.5) marks ecological damage but is not the definitional threshold.

questions.stem: The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) derives its statutory authority to prescribe National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) and regulate air pollution primarily from:

options.option_text: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 — a broader umbrella statute
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 as amended in 1991
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974

questions.explanation: B is correct — the CPCB was constituted specifically under the Air Act, 1981, which also mandates State Pollution Control Boards to regulate industrial emissions and set ambient standards. Option A (EPA, 1986) is a common distractor because it grants broader environmental powers, but CPCB's specific air mandate flows from the 1981 Act. Option D is the Water Act, 1974, which established CPCB for water pollution before the Air Act extended its role.

questions.stem: Under India's National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), a city is designated a 'non-attainment city' if it has:

options.option_text: AQI recorded in 'Very Poor' or worse category for over 60 days a year
Exceeded NAAQS limits for PM₁₀ or PM₂.₅ for five or more consecutive years
Annual PM₂.₅ mean concentration above the WHO guideline of 15 µg/m³
Population above 10 lakh with no real-time AQI monitoring station

questions.explanation: B is correct — CPCB identifies non-attainment cities as those that have consistently failed India's own NAAQS (not WHO guidelines) for particulate matter over at least five continuous years. 122 such cities were listed under NCAP (2019). Option C is a common confusion: the WHO 2021 guideline of 15 µg/m³ is more stringent than NAAQS (annual limit: 40 µg/m³), but non-attainment status is judged against domestic NAAQS, not WHO targets.

questions.stem: In Indian air quality regulations and health literature, the term 'Respirable Suspended Particulate Matter' (RSPM) specifically refers to airborne particles with an aerodynamic diameter not exceeding:

options.option_text: 2.5 micrometres — ultra-fine particles that reach the deep alveoli
10 micrometres — particles deposited in the upper respiratory tract
50 micrometres — coarse dust that settles near emission sources
100 micrometres — total suspended particles including heavy grit

questions.explanation: B is correct — RSPM corresponds to PM₁₀, particles ≤10 µm that can pass through the nose and throat to reach the bronchi and upper lung. Option A describes PM₂.₅ (fine particles penetrating to alveoli), which is a sub-fraction of RSPM. Examiners frequently use 'RSPM' expecting students to know it equals PM₁₀ = 10 µm cut-off, not PM₂.₅.

questions.stem: Under India's Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) for Delhi-NCR, Stage IV emergency restrictions — including halting construction, banning entry of BS-IV diesel trucks, and considering school closures — are triggered when the 24-hour average AQI crosses:

options.option_text: 300 — the lower boundary of the 'Very Poor' AQI category
350 — a sub-threshold used for anticipatory early-warning notices
400 — the entry point into the 'Severe' AQI category band
450 — the 'Severe+' sub-threshold within the Severe AQI band

questions.explanation: D is correct — GRAP Stage IV ('Emergency') is invoked at AQI > 450 (Severe+), one step above Stage III which covers AQI 401–450. This is a frequent source of error: candidates confuse Stage III (AQI 401–450, Severe) with Stage IV (AQI > 450). Option C (400) triggers only Stage III restrictions. The Supreme Court-mandated GRAP framework was revised in 2022 to make sub-stage thresholds more precise.

questions.stem: The 'Ozone Depleting Potential' (ODP) of any substance is expressed relative to a universally agreed reference compound whose ODP is defined as 1.0. That reference compound is:

options.option_text: CFC-12 (dichlorodifluoromethane) — the most widely produced refrigerant
Halon-1301 (bromotrifluoromethane) — used in aircraft fire suppression
CFC-11 (trichlorofluoromethane) — the agreed benchmark for the ODP scale
HCFC-22 (chlorodifluoromethane) — a transitional replacement refrigerant

questions.explanation: C is correct — CFC-11 (CCl₃F, also called Freon-11) is the international reference substance with ODP = 1.0 under the Montreal Protocol framework. All other ODS are benchmarked against it: e.g., Halon-1301 has ODP ~10, CFC-12 ~0.82, HCFC-22 ~0.034. Option A (CFC-12) is a common distractor because it was more commercially prevalent, but CFC-11 was chosen as the reference due to its simpler structure and well-characterised stratospheric chemistry.
